title: AI use amplifies professional liability risks (with sidebar: Insurers cautious on E&O exclusions)
author: Matthew Lerner

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on selective, task-appropriate deployment and meaningful verification, and materially extends it by showing how failures create professional-liability exposure and affect insurance coverage and underwriting.
qs: Many professionals may be creating “a real exposure for errors and omissions” if they are using AI to create efficiencies without properly vetting the output to ensure it is without hallucinations or information gaps, said Maria Long, New York-based chief underwriting officer at cyber insurer Resilience.
She noted that some AI tools are built for specific professions, including law, and that practitioners must use the appropriate application.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by treating human verification and appropriate tool selection as continuing professional responsibilities, while presenting insurance as conditional on policy wording rather than a substitute for those duties. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that malpractice claims remain limited and that competitive conditions currently restrain exclusions and tighter underwriting.
qs: Many professionals may be creating “a real exposure for errors and omissions” if they are using AI to create efficiencies without properly vetting the output to ensure it is without hallucinations or information gaps, said Maria Long, New York-based chief underwriting officer at cyber insurer Resilience.

Most E&O and cyber liability policies are written broadly enough to cover errors in professional services or security and privacy failures, regardless of the technology involved, unless they include a specific AI exclusion, said Kara Higginbotham, New York-based head of professional liability and cyber at Zurich North America.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by distinguishing already-reported sanctions from still-limited malpractice claims, treating further claims growth as predictive, and generally characterising AI-related negligence as covered absent a specific exclusion. It also reinforces the synthesis’s emphasis on verification failures, underwriting visibility and policy-specific uncertainty.

kp.k: Unverified AI outputs heighten professional liability exposure
kp.d: Insurance executives argue that professionals, including lawyers and doctors, increase errors-and-omissions exposure when they use AI for efficiency without verification for hallucinations or information gaps. This is presented as an expert risk assessment rather than a quantified finding.
qs: Many professionals may be creating “a real exposure for errors and omissions” if they are using AI to create efficiencies without properly vetting the output to ensure it is without hallucinations or information gaps, said Maria Long, New York-based chief underwriting officer at cyber insurer Resilience.
AI can significantly heighten professional liability risk for many types of firms, said Melissa Sowa, New York-based managing director of errors and omissions product line leadership at Markel.

kp.k: AI misconduct has already emerged in legal practice
kp.d: Gallagher’s Laura Zaroski reports regular legal-sector incidents in which attorneys file hallucinated case law without reviewing it. She says courts sometimes impose monetary sanctions of $1,000 or $5,000, which insurance does not cover.
qs: “It’s not emerging, it’s definitely emerged,” in the law firm sector she said, with regular reports of “hallucinated” case law not reviewed by attorneys being filed with courts and sometimes drawing modest monetary sanctions of $1,000 or $5,000.
Such fines are not covered by insurance, Ms. Zaroski said.

kp.k: Legal malpractice claims remain limited but may rise
kp.d: Zaroski distinguishes existing court-sanction incidents from legal malpractice claims: she says relatively few malpractice claims have appeared so far but predicts that more are coming. The document provides no claims count, sample, or loss data supporting the forecast.
qs: Although claims remain limited so far, that could change, she said.
“We haven’t seen too many legal malpractice claims … I think they’re coming.”

kp.k: Existing malpractice policies generally cover AI-caused negligence
kp.d: The interviewed insurance specialists say AI-related mistakes generally fall within existing legal professional liability or E&O coverage unless a policy expressly excludes AI. Professionals remain responsible for tool-caused mistakes, while insurers generally retain their coverage obligations.
qs: “They’re covered like any other act, error, or omission that you would see covered under a legal malpractice policy; it’s just like having a bad first-year associate or misreading a case,” Ms. Zaroski said.

Unless a policy specifically excludes AI, professionals remain responsible for mistakes caused by the tools they use, and insurers generally remain responsible for coverage, said Michael Carr, Chicago-based head of cyber portfolio underwriting, North America, for Coalition.
Standard E&O policies, including Markel’s, generally cover AI-related negligence arising from professional services, Ms. Sowa said.

kp.k: Some insurers offer affirmative AI coverage endorsements
kp.d: Markel permits brokers to add express AI coverage to its miscellaneous E&O form through an endorsement, but that coverage is subject to a sublimit. More broadly, Zurich’s Kara Higginbotham says technology-neutral E&O and cyber wordings commonly cover professional errors and security or privacy failures unless specifically excluding AI.
qs: She added that Markel’s miscellaneous E&O form allows brokers to add affirmative AI coverage via an endorsement, subject to a sublimit.

Most E&O and cyber liability policies are written broadly enough to cover errors in professional services or security and privacy failures, regardless of the technology involved, unless they include a specific AI exclusion, said Kara Higginbotham, New York-based head of professional liability and cyber at Zurich North America.

kp.k: Rising claims could produce exclusions or coverage limits
kp.d: Zaroski predicts that increased AI-related claims activity could lead insurers to exclude AI, limit exposure, or define coverage more expressly. This is conditional speculation about future policy wording, not evidence that widespread exclusions have already occurred.
qs: Such claims would likely fall under legal professional liability coverage, but a rise in claims activity could prompt insurers to limit their exposure, Ms. Zaroski said.
“If we keep seeing an increase in claims, we may see more carriers potentially putting in some exclusions.”

“If we still keep seeing this increase in claims, we may see more carriers potentially putting in some exclusions, limiting their exposure, or somehow either assertively covering it or assertively not covering it in creative ways in the future,” said Laura Zaroski, Chicago-based managing director, law firms practice, at Arthur J. Gallagher.

kp.k: Shadow AI complicates error attribution and underwriting
kp.d: Long argues that AI embedded in ordinary workflows, including unauthorized or undisclosed shadow IT, will make it difficult to identify how a professional error occurred. Higginbotham separately warns that underwriting may fail to capture additional risk when insurers do not understand an organization’s actual AI adoption and use.
qs: As AI becomes more embedded in everyday workflows, identifying the true source of an error may become more difficult, Ms. Long said.
“It’s going to be very difficult to try to parse out how the error or omission actually happened,” Ms. Long said.
“There’s a whole lot of shadow IT being used when it comes to leveraging artificial intelligence, and you can’t always tell when it’s been a part of the professional service journey, so to speak.”

She added, however, “there could be additional risk presented by AI that is not contemplated if there is a lack of awareness or understanding of how an insured organization is using or adopting AI when making an underwriting decision.”

kp.k: Lawyers must select appropriate tools and verify outputs
kp.d: Axa XL’s Michelle Chia says professionals must choose tools suited to their specific field and task. Failure to vet both the tool and its output may be treated as an error or omission, analogous to relying on an untrained associate or releasing work without review.
qs: Professionals must also choose the right AI tool for each task, said Michelle Chia, New York-based chief underwriting officer for cyber in the Americas at Axa XL.
She noted that some AI tools are built for specific professions, including law, and that practitioners must use the appropriate application.

Failing to properly vet an AI tool and its output could be treated much like relying on untrained associates or publishing unreviewed work and could ultimately be viewed as an error or omission, Ms. Chia said.

“There are general tools that have not been trained on specific data, and so to use that tool for professional service, any type of professional service would be a disservice to the client,” Ms. Chia said.

kp.k: AI technology providers receive greater underwriting scrutiny
kp.d: Coalition reports applying more intensive underwriting scrutiny to technology companies that supply AI products or services than to typical technology E&O accounts. The source does not specify the additional information requested or quantify the underwriting difference.
qs: Coalition is paying closer attention to underwriting technology companies that offer AI products or services.
“We are asking a lot more of them than we are on our typical tech errors and omissions account,” Mr. Carr said.

kp.k: Insurance competition discourages immediate AI exclusions
kp.d: The sidebar reports that soft-market competition makes insurers reluctant to add AI exclusions, questionnaires, or other underwriting friction before substantial claims emerge. Brokers are expected to resist exclusions while competing carriers continue to cover AI risks or remain silent about them.
qs: Underwriters may be reluctant to add exclusions for artificial intelligence in errors and omissions policies due to concerns that their products will be less attractive in a competitive market, they said.

“You’re not going to see a lot of additional friction introduced into the underwriting process for any product until you start to see some claims, because there are commercial concerns around friction,” said Michael Carr, Chicago-based head of cyber portfolio underwriting, North America, for Coalition.
“In a soft market, it’s extremely challenging to ask any more questions,” said Maria Long, New York-based chief underwriting officer at cyber insurer Resilience.

“It’s very competitive, so brokers are unlikely to accept AI exclusions when other insurers are offering coverage or silent regarding AI,” said Melissa Sowa, New York-based managing director, errors and omissions, product line leadership, for Markel.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI use can increase professional liability exposure when professionals fail to verify outputs or choose appropriate tools.
pts.d: Matthew Lerner frames AI adoption as creating heightened exposures in professions including law and medicine. Resilience’s Maria Long identifies unverified hallucinations and information gaps as sources of errors-and-omissions exposure. Markel’s Melissa Sowa says AI can significantly heighten professional liability risk. Axa XL’s Michelle Chia argues that practitioners must select task-appropriate tools and verify both tools and outputs; failures could be treated like reliance on untrained associates or publication of unreviewed work.

pts.k: AI-related misconduct has already appeared in courts, and legal malpractice claims are expected to follow.
pts.d: Gallagher’s Laura Zaroski describes regular reports of attorneys filing unreviewed, fabricated case law, sometimes resulting in monetary sanctions of $1,000 or $5,000. She states that these fines are uninsured. She distinguishes these existing incidents from legal malpractice claims, which she says remain limited but predicts will increase.

pts.k: AI-related professional negligence generally falls within existing liability coverage, absent a specific exclusion.
pts.d: Zaroski says AI-related legal malpractice would likely be covered as an ordinary professional error. Coalition’s Michael Carr says professionals remain responsible for mistakes caused by their tools and insurers generally remain responsible for coverage unless AI is specifically excluded. Sowa says standard E&O policies, including Markel’s, generally cover AI-related professional negligence; Markel also offers an affirmative AI endorsement under its miscellaneous E&O form, subject to a sublimit. Zurich’s Kara Higginbotham describes most E&O and cyber policies as technology-neutral in their coverage of professional errors and security or privacy failures, subject to specific exclusions.

pts.k: Growing claims could trigger AI exclusions or coverage restrictions, but insurance-market competition currently discourages them.
pts.d: Zaroski predicts that increasing claims could lead insurers to limit exposure, add exclusions, or make AI coverage more explicit. Carr says commercial concerns discourage additional underwriting friction before claims materialize. Long describes additional questions as particularly difficult in a soft market. Sowa says brokers are unlikely to accept AI exclusions while competitors offer coverage or leave AI unaddressed explicitly.

pts.k: Embedded and undisclosed AI use can obscure error attribution and leave underwriting risks unidentified.
pts.d: Long predicts that identifying how an error occurred will become harder as AI enters everyday workflows, citing shadow IT and difficulty detecting AI’s involvement in professional services. Higginbotham warns that incomplete understanding of an insured organization’s AI adoption may leave additional risks unanticipated in underwriting. Carr reports that Coalition already applies greater scrutiny to technology companies offering AI products or services than to typical technology E&O accounts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of insurance practitioners’ observations, professional judgments, and descriptions of coverage and underwriting practices.
pts.d: The article supplies no quantitative claims dataset, measured hallucination rate, benchmark, named court case, or reproduced policy wording. Zaroski supports the legal-risk discussion with reports of fabricated case-law filings and illustrative sanction amounts, while acknowledging few malpractice claims so far. Coverage claims rest on the speakers’ professional authority and Sowa’s description of Markel’s policy offering. Carr provides a company-specific account of heightened underwriting scrutiny. Predictions of future claims and exclusions are expressed as judgments or conditional possibilities, not measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes existing misconduct and current coverage practices from undated, conditional predictions about malpractice claims and insurance restrictions.
pts.d: As of the article’s June 26, 2026 publication, Zaroski describes court-filing misconduct as already present but malpractice claims as limited. No date or numerical forecast is supplied for future claims. Restrictions are conditional on increased claims activity and constrained by competitive or soft-market conditions. Current coverage descriptions are qualified by policy terms, specific AI exclusions, and the sublimit on Markel’s affirmative endorsement. Long’s attribution concern is prospective as AI becomes more embedded; Higginbotham’s warning depends on underwriters lacking awareness of AI use.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern professional-service providers and clients, liability insurers and brokers, and AI technology suppliers.
pts.d: Law firms and attorneys face responsibility for unverified AI work, uninsured sanctions, possible malpractice claims, and potentially narrower future coverage. Other professionals, including medical practitioners, face analogous E&O exposures. Clients are affected by unsuitable tools or unchecked outputs in professional services. Insurers face potentially greater claims exposure, incomplete visibility into AI use, and competitive constraints on underwriting and exclusions. Brokers and policyholders face possible additional questionnaires and coverage restrictions. AI product and service companies are a distinct group already receiving heightened technology E&O scrutiny at Coalition; they are not identified as alternative legal service providers.
